groupedByStatusNoFilters.ownerVerdict: 'The cards are fine but the filtering is just not working.' Owner chose grouping over any filter arrangement.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.rootCause: Not styling. Status became TYPE-DEPENDENT once the owner asked for Answered/Closed and Active/No longer active — 8 values across 4 lifecycles. Two side-by-side filters only work when the axes are independent, and these are not: 'Answered' is meaningless for a banner, 'No longer active' is meaningless for a general question. A flat status row would list 8 values, most irrelevant to whatever the person is looking at. Three iterations of styling (outline, then What's New's plain + menu, then plain + separator) were all treating a modelling problem as a visual one.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.shipped: No filter controls at all. Sections: NEEDS YOU · IN REVIEW · ACTIVE · DONE, newest first within each. Group names are type-agnostic; the precise per-type status stays on the card badge. NEEDS YOU leads because it is the only group holding work.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.statusVocabularyPerType: Dashboard (Add/Edit/Remove): Pending review → Approved · Rejected. Dashboard (Promote) and Banner: Pending review → Approved → Active → No longer active, or Rejected — a lifecycle beyond approval that nothing else in the flow has. General: Pending review → Answered · Closed. Any type, any time: Needs your reply. Feature Request has no status here at all. Written into the spec as 'do not build one flat enum'.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.noResultsFrameDeleted: With no filters, an empty page can only mean the person has never filed a request — so there is ONE empty state, not two. The 'no results for these filters' frame and half of its spec note went with the filter bar.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.cloneDefectsCaughtByScreenshot: Two new cards were cloned to demonstrate the new statuses, and both carried their source's data: #0402 and #0405 kept the ORIGINAL cards' dates (08/29, 09/01) which broke the newest-first order, and #0405 was cloned from the only card WITHOUT an admin note, so the note lookup found nothing and skipped silently — the card shipped with no note while the write reported success. A findOne that returns null is not an error; check the count when a clone is supposed to carry a part.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.openQuestion: No search. Grouping scales to a screen or two; past that, finding a request by name or reference number needs one. Recorded in Still open.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.lint: All 30 frames, eight checks, zero findings.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.searchAdded: A single full-width search field at the top, the only control on the page. Placeholder 'Search requests by name or reference number…' — the reference number is searchable on purpose, since the confirmation hands it over and the failure copy tells people to quote it. Deliberately NOT on the heading row beside New request: it is a control over the list, so it belongs above the list, not next to a page action.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.liveVersusPastDivider: A horizontal Separator between ACTIVE and DONE, wrapped in a frame with 16px top and bottom padding so the gap is 48px against the 32px that separates groups. The extra space is load-bearing: at an even gap the rule read as one more group boundary rather than the single division that matters. Above it everything is live, below it everything is finished.
groupedByStatusNoFilters.ownerEditPickedUp: The first group heading read 'NEEDS YOUR REPLY' rather than the 'NEEDS YOU' that was built — an owner edit made in the file. Kept, because it matches the status badge word for word, and the group FRAME was renamed to match so the two cannot drift.

requestDetailView.frame: 'Request detail — needs your reply' — built on #0416, the banner request the admin team has asked a question about, because that is the case the detail view exists for.
requestDetailView.threeParts: Back link · heading (reference, type, title, status badge, submitted date) · a read-only card of EVERY submitted field · an Activity thread ending in a reply composer.
requestDetailView.whyTheSubmittedFieldsCardIsNotOptional: A person is being asked a question about a request they filed days ago. Without their own answers in front of them they cannot answer it. The Banner example renders all seven fields including the call-to-action URL — a summary would not be enough.
requestDetailView.threadClosesTheStatusLoop: Entries carry author and timestamp, oldest first, and include system entries ('Submitted this request'), admin notes and the person's replies. Sending a reply moves the request off 'Needs your reply' back to 'In review'; an admin reply moves it the other way. That loop is the entire reason the status exists — without the detail view the status could be set but never cleared.
requestDetailView.componentsUsed: Avatar (sm, circle, initials fallback) for thread authors, Card for both panels, the confirmation's label/value row as the submitted-fields row, Separator above the composer, Textarea + Button for the reply. No custom parts.
requestDetailView.gotchaClonedTextareaCollapsed: The reply Textarea was cloned from the Banner form where it sat in a row with layoutSizingVertical FILL. In the composer's VERTICAL stack that collapsed the instance to 52px while its inner ui-input-wrap--multi stayed 100px — a 74px spill that drew the Send button on top of the field. Every property read correct; only the render and the instance-spill check showed it. Set layoutSizingVertical HUG after cloning a field out of a row.
requestDetailView.openQuestion: Whether a DONE request keeps its composer. Leaving it open invites replies to a closed decision with nobody watching; removing it strands someone with a follow-up. Likely answer is a read-only thread plus a 'Start a new request' action — owner call. Recorded in Still open.
requestDetailView.lint: All 31 frames, eight checks, zero findings.

page102Navigation2026_09_02.trigger: Owner spotted that the new Request-detail view had a 'Back to My requests' button, contradicting the earlier recorded decision 'Back button REMOVED — Cancel in the submit bar is the single exit.' They asked for the genuinely best and most consistent answer rather than a revert.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.theRule: Every screen below a Sidebar item carries a Breadcrumb rooted at that item. There is NO Cancel button anywhere in the request flow. You leave by navigating, and one guard catches every route out of unsaved work.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.whyTheEarlierDecisionWasReversed: 'Cancel is the single exit' was correct for a standalone page and is VOID inside the application shell on page 103 (frame 1837:44): a 48px AppRail of applications, a 256px 'Sidebar — DART Central' whose items include My Requests, and a browser-style TabStrip of open windows. A dirty form there already has four exits that never touch Cancel — Sidebar item, rail, tab switch, tab close. So the guard cannot belong to a button; it must fire on ANY navigation away from unsaved work. Once that is true a breadcrumb is not a second door, it is the door the shell already opens — and Cancel becomes the duplicate. Cancel went, the breadcrumb stayed.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.noConventionExistedToMatch: Research found the library has NO navigation guidance: Breadcrumb is the only Navigation-group component with no usage.when/usage.avoid block, CLAUDE.md has no back/cancel/breadcrumb routing rule, and the Figma 'Choosing components' page has no navigation section. The only precedent is BillingHandoff and ConsoleDashboard, which both place a 2-level Breadcrumb directly above the page title. The ghost back BUTTON was the pattern the library had used nowhere — which is why it read as drift.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.built: 21 breadcrumbs added from the assembled set Breadcrumb (1552:434), Glyph=chevron, as the first child of each content column. 2 levels on the detail view and the chooser; 3 on every form, the submitting state and the failure state. 20 Cancel instances removed; the chooser's now-empty submit bar removed with them.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.deliberateOmissions: No breadcrumb on My Requests list or its empty state (they ARE the Sidebar item — a one-level crumb says nothing), on the scope-menu spec frame, or on either confirmation. Confirmations are terminal outcomes rather than locations, their forward actions already name the destinations, and the feature confirmation must not root at 'My requests' since feature requests never appear there.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.crumbLabelIsTheFormNotTheTab: The Dashboard crumb reads 'Dashboard Request', not the active tab — the tab strip is the mode switch, consistent with the earlier decision that retitled that frame.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.guardMovedToNavigation: ⑤ dialog case 2 renamed CANCEL — DIRTY FORM → LEAVING A DIRTY FORM; its copy was already accurate for navigation. A fifth case added, DETAIL — UNSENT REPLY ('Discard your reply?' → Keep editing / Discard reply) — without it the detail view was the one screen where typed work died silently. ③ Behavior spec rewritten to state that the guard belongs to navigation, not a control, and that navigation is blocked while a submit is in flight since Cancel used to be the disabled control that said so.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.flaggedNotDone: Page 102 frames are 1072 wide; the shell's 'Main Content — not built yet' is 1308. Every screen needs re-fitting when it moves in. Also: Dashboard modes live in Tabs while the other three types live behind the chooser, so 'change my request type' has two mechanisms — pre-existing.
page102Navigation2026_09_02.verification: Zero Cancel instances outside the dialog panel. All 21 breadcrumbs assert correct Levels, labels, first crumb Type=link and last Type=current, positioned as first child. Eight-check lint across all 31 frames: zero findings. page102Sizing2026_09_02.trigger: Owner asked what the right design width is before fitting page 102 into the shell, accounting for all desktop sizes (mobile out of scope).
page102Sizing2026_09_02.theInstructionWasWrongAndMeasuringShowed: 'Fit the frames to 1308' would have changed nothing but the width of the empty gutters: every form frame already caps its content column at 672 (--max-w-2xl) and the list/detail at 880, FILL-sized inside a CENTER-aligned frame. The deliverable was a sizing MODEL, not a frame width.
page102Sizing2026_09_02.designViewport1440: 1440 − 304 chrome (AppRail 48 + Sidebar 256) = 1136, which sits 16px under the library's own app-shell cap --max-w-6xl (1152, used by SuitePage, SuitePageV2 and both DeeperTheming stories). Designing at the cap means everything wider only grows gutters and everything narrower is a visible reflow. At 1280 — the current figma-playbook width — Main is 976, BELOW the cap, which would hide the fact that content can grow at all.
page102Sizing2026_09_02.shipped: All 25 screen frames on page 102 resized 1072 → 1136. Page 103's two shell frames resized 1612 → 1440; v12 (built from components) now reports Main Content exactly 1136. Doc panels and the scope-menu detail frame deliberately left at their own widths.
page102Sizing2026_09_02.provedNothingReflowed: Captured inner geometry before and after: every element shifted by exactly +32px — half the 64px width increase — with identical widths (672, 304, 624, 880, 832, 104, 142). Pure re-centring. That is the check that distinguishes 'the frame got wider' from 'the layout changed'.
page102Sizing2026_09_02.supportedRange: Owner chose a 1024 floor. Three shell rules and nothing else: collapse the Sidebar to icon under 1280, hide the AppRail under 1024 (the DartCentralHome.scss:113 precedent), Drawer under 768 (already shipped). Content reflow points: form column shrinks below Main 800, list/detail below Main 1008. Gutter 64, floored at 24 below 1024.

correctionOnRecord.whatIGotWrong: I described the library as 'effectively non-responsive by design' while presenting options, which alarmed the owner and changed their answer.
correctionOnRecord.whatIsActuallyTrue: The components are FLUID and container-driven. Measured across all 65 component stylesheets: 42 use width:100% / flex / grid; only TWO hardcoded pixel widths exist in the entire library (TabBar min-width 140, Toast min-width 300, both documented panel geometry); 40 auto-fit/auto-fill grids reflow continuously with no breakpoint to keep in sync; 37 logical-property usages. What the library does not carry is PAGE-LEVEL breakpoints, which is correct — a component library should not dictate page layout. The five media queries that exist are exactly the cases where a component must know the viewport.
correctionOnRecord.lesson: 'Few media queries' is not 'not responsive'. Intrinsic fluidity is the stronger form of responsive, because there is no breakpoint to keep in sync. Do not summarise a measurement as a judgement.

page102Sizing2026_09_02.libraryGapStillOpen: The one real breakpoint (768) is expressed three ways with nothing tying them together: SIDEBAR_MOBILE_BREAKPOINT, the useIsMobile default, and two hand-written @media (max-width: 767px) literals in Chat.scss and AidenPanel.scss. Prototypes independently invented 640 and 1023, docs chrome 1100. Separately, --max-w-screen-sm/md/lg/xl/2xl are DEAD — nothing consumes them and custom properties are invalid inside @media by definition, so they advertise a breakpoint system that does not exist.
page102Sizing2026_09_02.verification: All 25 screen frames report 1136; every content column still 672 or 880 with maxWidth intact; padding still 128. Shell frames 1440 with Main Content 1136. Eight-check lint across all 31 frames: zero findings. No section overlaps. Screenshotted.

twoViewportsDrawn.why: Owner: big monitors here, so make sure max-widths do not make wide screens look off. That is not answerable from a rule — it has to be seen. Sections 1–7 are 1440 (Main 1136); new section 8 holds the same screens at 1920 (Main 1616).
twoViewportsDrawn.capsDidNotRise: Measured rather than judged: on a list card at 880 the title starts at x80 and the status badge at x726 — already 646px apart. At a 1152 cap that becomes ~918px, so a request's status drifts further from the request it describes. The descriptions are single-line at 880, so extra width buys nothing and costs scanning. Raising the cap would have made the cards emptier, not fuller. The form stays 672 for the ordinary reason: a wider form is a worse form.
twoViewportsDrawn.whatChangesAtWideIsLayoutNotWidth: The request detail goes TWO COLUMN above roughly 1600 Main — submitted details fixed 600, activity thread filling the rest, 24px gap. It is the one screen where the extra space carries content instead of padding: you read the admin's question and the fields it is about at the same time, and the frame drops from 939px tall to 647 so it fits without scrolling. The list and forms stay single-column and centred at every width.
twoViewportsDrawn.lesson: 'Looks empty on a big monitor' is usually not a cap problem. Check what the content does with the width first: if descriptions are single-line and a right-aligned control is already far from its label, widening makes both worse. The fix is a layout that uses the axis, not a bigger number.

staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.whatTheOwnerSaw: After the detail view was narrowed from 880 to 600 for the two-column wide layout, their Figma client showed the left card's values clipped mid-word at the card edge ('Collateral Health Dashb', 'briefly unavaila').
staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.actualState: A stale render. Re-measured: the value text nodes are 376 wide ending at x576 inside a 600 card, and a fresh screenshot wraps correctly with nothing clipped. Figma had recomputed the FILL widths after the write; the client had not repainted. This is the fifth stale-measurement/stale-render event in this file after a sizing change.
staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.theRealFinding: The instance-spill lint COULD NOT have caught it even if it had been real. It compares only an instance's DIRECT children against the instance bounds, so a TEXT node two levels down — inside a SLOT, inside a row — is invisible to it. Every clipped-text bug of this shape would pass.
staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.checkAdded: A deep clip sweep: for every node with clipsContent (including the frame itself), walk ALL descendants and flag any whose bounding box crosses the clipper on any edge, skipping nodes already governed by a nearer clipping ancestor. Run across all 34 frames: zero clipped nodes.
staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.lesson: A spill check that stops at direct children only catches spills the container cannot hide. Clipping is precisely the case where the container DOES hide it, so the check has to be depth-first from every clipper, not one level from every instance.
staleRenderAndTheLintGapItExposed.CORRECTION: I called this a stale render. It was not — the owner had already repaired the frame, so the geometry I measured was THEIR fix, not a self-healed state. The clipping was real. Lesson: when a report and a measurement disagree, establish whether anything changed the file between them before concluding the report was wrong. The deep clip sweep added here is still the right outcome, and would have caught it.

page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.myBug: When I re-fitted the frames to 1136 I re-laid every section with sort((a,b) => a.y - b.y), which flattened each into ONE column ordered by whatever stale y-position the frames happened to have. Dashboard came out add → edit → promote → remove → edit → promote → remove → promote → remove → add. Outcome came out confirmation → failed → submitting → feature. A sort is not a layout: it preserves nothing about meaning.
page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.dashboardIsNowOneColumnPerTab: The section documents four modes behind a Tabs strip, so it now reads as four parallel branches — ADD · EDIT · PROMOTE · REMOVE, left to right in tab order, each column running top to bottom through its own states. Labelled column headers state the gate: Add has no dashboard picker; Edit, Promote and Remove are gated on picking one; Promote and Remove then need more required fields, which is why they have a third frame and Edit does not.
page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.outcomeIsARowBecauseItIsASequence: Submitting → Request submitted (Dashboard/Banner/General) → Request submitted (feature) → Submission failed, left to right. A column implied these were alternatives at the same level; a row reads as the sequence it is, and matches stage 3 of the ④ Flow map.
page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.bannerDetailMovedLast: The scope-menu spec frame had sorted into second place, interrupting no-type → standard → custom. It is a component detail, not a step, so it sits after the three screens.
page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.principle: Section layout has to encode the flow: a COLUMN means 'these follow one another', a ROW of columns means 'these are parallel branches', and a ROW of frames means 'this is a sequence'. Position is the only thing a developer scanning the canvas can read before opening anything.
page102ReadingOrder2026_09_02.verification: Reading order asserted per section. Deep clip sweep: 0. Eight-check lint across all 34 frames: 0. No section overlaps, nothing loose.

adminFlow2026_09_02.what: The other half of the request loop, on the Figma page 'Admin Flow' (previously empty). 7 frames in 3 sections: one Approval Queue plus a scoped variant and an empty state, two request-review screens, an action-dialogs panel and a read-first doc panel.
adminFlow2026_09_02.ownerDecisions: ONE queue at the DART Admin level grouped by product, not one per product. Feature requests never enter the queue — the public backlog is the triage. Request-review path only; Control Center, Banners, Feature Flags, Redirects, Analytics, Access Control and Changelog are separate admin surfaces, explicitly out.

theLoopIsTheProduct.mapping: Approve → Approved (or Active once a banner/promotion goes live) · Deny → Rejected · Request more information → Needs your reply, the top group on My requests · requester replies → back to In review, which returns it to the queue.
theLoopIsTheProduct.notAdminOnlyNotes: The deny reason and the more-information message are written straight into the requester's activity thread and are the only thing they receive — there is no email. Both dialogs make their field required for that reason.
theLoopIsTheProduct.asserted: Every admin verb in the frames appears in the doc's mapping table, and every requester status the table names exists in the Request Flow behavior spec. Checked programmatically, not by eye.

adminFlow2026_09_02.actionBarIsTypeDependent: Dashboard and Banner: Approve · Request more information · Deny. General: Answer · Request more information · Close. A General request is a question, and the requester's own vocabulary already says Answered/Closed rather than Approved/Rejected — one action bar for all three types would ship a wrong verb. Both review frames are drawn so the difference is visible rather than inferred.
adminFlow2026_09_02.stylingFollowsTheStatusNotThePosition: Deny is an error outline because it produces Rejected. Close is a quiet ghost because it produces Closed — a question that needed no answer is not a rejection, and dressing it in red would tell the requester something untrue. Deny/Close sit apart from the two constructive actions so neither is clicked on the way to Approve.
adminFlow2026_09_02.reuseNotLookalike: Every screen was cloned from its requester counterpart rather than rebuilt. Asserted: the queue's row cards resolve to the SAME mainComponent id as My Requests' cards (1811:796), and each row's FeaturedIcon colour + glyph match the chooser's option cards exactly. That is the check that distinguishes reuse from something that merely looks the same.
adminFlow2026_09_02.noBreadcrumbOnTheQueue: Approval Queue is itself a sidebar item, so it takes no breadcrumb — the same rule that gives My Requests none. The review screens carry 'Approval Queue › #0417'.
gotchas: A clone from a Banner request carried the amber bell icon onto a Dashboard review — icons must be swapped per type, not inherited.
findAll(TEXT) on a thread entry returns the AVATAR's own text node first, so index-based assignment wrote the body text into the meta line. Target by node name.
Fresh-clone findAll missed the summary rows again (fifth occurrence); re-fetching the node by id and reading .children worked.

Dialog footer buttons are named 'Button', not 'ui-button', so a name-prefix selector matched nothing and silently left the discard-dialog labels in place. Select them by mainComponent.parent.name === 'Button'.
The cloned dialogs inherited error-variant confirms; Approve and Send question had to be swapped back to default.
adminFlow2026_09_02.openItems: No history view for requests already decided — the queue shows only what is waiting. No reassignment to another admin. Both recorded on the doc panel.
adminFlow2026_09_02.verification: Reading order asserted per section (queue as a column, the two review screens as a row of parallel type variants). Reuse and loop assertions pass. Eight-check lint 0 and deep clip sweep 0 across all 7 frames. No Cancel button on any admin screen.

controlCenterOverview.what: Added on owner request after the first cut deliberately excluded it. The admin's landing page — what DART Admin opens to — so it carries no breadcrumb, same rule as My Requests and the Approval Queue. Three stat tiles, a By Product section with a card per product administered, and a Recent Activity feed.
controlCenterOverview.numbersReconcile: The tiles and the per-product cards add up: 1+3+1 pending = the 5 on the tile, 1+2+1 banners = the 4, products managed = 3 = the number of product cards. A dashboard whose own totals disagree with its rows loses the reader immediately, so this is stated on the doc panel as a rule to preserve when real data arrives.
controlCenterOverview.onlyOneMetricIsLive: 'Pending approvals' leads to the Approval Queue, which exists. Active banners and published dashboards point at admin surfaces that were explicitly excluded from this cut. Drawn because the overview is the owner's own reference, but labelled on the doc panel as placeholders rather than a spec for undesigned pages.
controlCenterOverview.recentActivityIsTheNearestThingToHistory: Four rows covering approve / request-more-info / a new submission / deny, each with product, timestamp and the resulting status badge. The queue shows only what is waiting, so this feed is currently the only view of decisions already made — recorded as an open gap.

gotchaGlyphKeepsAnInheritedVariableBindi.symptom: After swapping a cloned FeaturedIcon to Color=blue, the tile rendered blue but the GLYPH stayed amber. Two more icons had the same fault in the opposite direction and looked fine to the eye.
gotchaGlyphKeepsAnInheritedVariableBindi.cause: swapComponent updates the tile, but the nested glyph's VECTOR keeps its inherited variable binding — DART Central's stroke was bound to #fbbf24 while a clean blue variant binds #0b63f3. The binding survives the swap; it is not an override that can be cleared.
gotchaGlyphKeepsAnInheritedVariableBindi.fix: Do not swap a cloned FeaturedIcon. Create a FRESH instance of the target variant, insert it at the old node's index, remove the old, then swap the glyph. Verified by comparing each icon's vector stroke against a clean instance of the same variant.
gotchaGlyphKeepsAnInheritedVariableBindi.whyTheEyeMissedIt: Only amber-on-blue was obvious. Blue-on-amber and amber-on-violet read as acceptable at a glance — comparing the rendered colour to the variant's own binding caught all three; looking at the screenshot caught one.

controlCenterOverview.gotchaIndexOfAcrossTheProxy: parent.children.indexOf(node) returns -1, so insertChild threw. Use findIndex(c => c.id === node.id). Third occurrence in this file.
controlCenterOverview.gotchaStaleFillAfterRebuild: Replacing the icon left one product card's inner frame at 312 wide inside an 880 slot despite reporting FILL. Setting FILL again did nothing; the FIXED → resize → FILL round-trip fixed it. Sixth stale-sizing event in this file.
controlCenterOverview.verification: 8 frames on the page. Eight-check lint 0, deep clip sweep 0. Section reading order: Overview leads, then the three queue states; review screens sit as a row of parallel type variants.

byProductRedesign.ownerFeedback: 'I don't like how the items are just chips — you can't see from here what the 1 pending is, that is an extra click.' Correct: a count with no content is a dead end, and the overview's whole job is to save that click.
byProductRedesign.shipped: The per-product CARD is gone. Each product is now a heading row — icon, name, status dot — and the ITEMS carry the containers underneath it. Every pending request is a real row with reference, type, requester, title, description, date and status badge. Five rows total, which is exactly the 5 on the Pending approvals tile.
byProductRedesign.whatStayedACount: Active banners and published dashboards remain a quiet link on the product's heading row ('2 active banners · 3 published dashboards ↗'). They are not actionable and their destinations are not built, so listing them would triple the page height to show things nobody can act on. The rule: what needs you gets a row, what does not gets a link.
byProductRedesign.overlapWithTheQueueIsDeliberate: The overview now lists the same pending requests the Approval Queue does. That is not duplication — the queue is the working surface (grouped by product, scoped, searchable) and the overview is the landing page that shows state at a glance. If they diverge later, the overview should show fewer rows with a 'view all' rather than a different set.
byProductRedesign.iconBugRecurredAndWasCaughtByAssertion: Every pending row inherited the donor's amber bell. Fixed by building fresh FeaturedIcon instances per request type — never a swap, per the binding lesson — and verified by comparing each row's vector stroke to a clean instance of the same variant.
byProductRedesign.gotchaProbeMustSitInsideTheFrame: The first verification pass reported ALL FIVE icons as mismatched, including ones just built correctly. The probe instances were parked on the page canvas, outside the frame that pins Mode=Dark — variable modes CASCADE, so a page-level probe resolves in light mode and every comparison fails. Park the probe inside the frame under test. A verification that fails everything is usually measuring itself, not the work.
byProductRedesign.gotchaDonorReferenceDies: Two runs aborted on 'node does not exist' / 'cannot read property clone of null' — a donor captured before a sibling removal is invalidated, and re-fetching by id did not survive either. The reliable pattern is to clone donors ONCE into a temporary holder frame on the same page, build from those, then delete the holder. Both aborted runs rolled back cleanly, which is worth knowing: a thrown plugin script leaves no partial state.

healthOverviewAndEstate.trigger: Owner: every example on the overview said Needs review or Waiting on requester, yet the summary claimed active banners and published dashboards — the active things were asserted and never shown. Plus scale: ~200 dashboards with additions constantly, and this person manages the whole site from here.
healthOverviewAndEstate.threeTiers: Rebuilt around the owner's own three questions — what must I action, where are the issues, what do I manage. Tiles are now Need your decision (5) · Issues to chase (3) · Dashboards live (201). Then NEEDS YOUR DECISION lists the five pending items, ISSUES TO CHASE lists the three problems, BY PRODUCT carries the inventory counts as links, and Recent Activity closes it.
healthOverviewAndEstate.whyCountsCameBackAfterBeingRemoved: Earlier the per-product chips were replaced with listed items because a count with no destination is a dead end. Counts are legitimate again now that the Dashboards table and Banners list EXIST — a number is only a dead end when it leads nowhere. The pending items stay listed because that is the thing you cannot infer from a number.
healthOverviewAndEstate.issuesAreDefinedNotDecorative: Owner picked three definitions: a banner past its end date but still displaying, a dashboard decommissioning soon, and a dashboard whose Tableau link failed its last check. They did NOT pick 'request aging past SLA'. The broken-link case depends on a health check the platform may not run — flagged when offered and chosen anyway, so it needs confirming that the data exists.

dashboardsTable.columns: Name · Project · Inventory · Status · Promoted · Banner · Added · actions. Status values Live / Decommissioning / Unreachable. Built from the Figma Table/HeaderCell and Table/Cell sets (text, code, badge, actions content variants).
dashboardsTable.aTableIsAThirdContentWidth: Forms cap at 672 and lists at 880, but a table is the one surface where more width is more information, so it takes the FULL Main Content minus gutters — 1008 at the 1440 design viewport. That is a third cap and it is deliberate.
dashboardsTable.eightColumnsBarelyFit: Measured need was 1036 against 1008 available — the header cells carry a sort chevron that was not budgeted for, and 'Decommissioning' makes the Status column 150 wide. Rather than shorten headers into nonsense, the Name column wraps to two lines (standard table behaviour) which frees the 28px. Worth knowing: eight columns is the ceiling at 1440; a ninth needs the 1920 viewport.
dashboardsTable.filterIsLegitimateHereUnlikeMyRequests: My Requests dropped its filters because status was TYPE-dependent — 'Answered' is meaningless for a banner. Every dashboard shares the same three states, so a status ToggleGroup filters something real. Same component, opposite conclusion, because the data model differs.
dashboardsTable.noSortOnActions: The actions column's header inherited a sort indicator. A column you cannot sort must not advertise that you can, so it is hidden.

healthOverviewAndEstate.bannersList: Active banners grouped by product, reusing the queue's grouped-list pattern. Includes the past-end-date banner that appears as an issue on the overview, so the two screens corroborate rather than merely coexist.
healthOverviewAndEstate.thirdCodeBlocker: Table exists in FIGMA ONLY — there is no src/components/Table and the owner chose Figma-only in August. The dashboards table is therefore a third code blocker alongside the Date component and the searchable multi-select Combobox. It also inherits Table's recorded open question: selected + hover has no token.
healthOverviewAndEstate.gotchaDonorsThatNoLongerExist: Cloning a ToggleGroup from the Request Flow page failed — those instances were deleted when My Requests moved to grouping. A donor that existed earlier in a session is not a donor now; create from the component set when the source screen has since changed.
healthOverviewAndEstate.verification: 10 frames across 4 sections. Eight-check lint 0 and deep clip sweep 0. Table columns re-measured against actual content after sizing, with zero cells exceeding their column.

overviewReferenceRebuild.trigger: Owner supplied a screenshot of the DART Central v11 prototype's Admin Overview and asked to chase it for the overview + approval queue, then clarified: 'don't rebuild it exactly, rebuild it with our components and tokens.'
overviewReferenceRebuild.ownerChoice: Match the reference model closely. ISSUES TO CHASE and BY PRODUCT were REMOVED. Flagged before building that this drops the decommissioning / past-end-date / broken-link surfacing from the landing page — it now lives only on the Banners and Dashboards screens. Chosen anyway.
overviewReferenceRebuild.renamed: 'Control Center Overview' -> 'Admin Overview', subtitle 'Platform-wide health across all DART products.' Control Center was an invented name; Admin matches the sidebar item the screen sits under.
overviewReferenceRebuild.tilesAreInventoryNow: Was the three questions (Need your decision / Issues to chase / Dashboards live). Now inventory: 4 Active banners (warning) · 5 Pending approvals (info) · 201 Dashboards live (success). Big 4xl/leading-none/Bold numeral over base-semibold title over sm-normal caption, inside the existing ui-card Size=xl — the reference's shape expressed with our card, our type ramp and status/{warning,info,success}/text, not a copied treatment.
overviewReferenceRebuild.didNotCopyTheThirdMetric: The reference's third tile is 'Promoted dashboards — via active feature flag'. There are no feature flags in this model and the Dashboards table shows exactly ONE Promoted row, so shipping the reference's 2 would have contradicted the table on the next click. Used 201 Dashboards live, which the Dashboards screen already states. Copying a number you cannot corroborate is the failure the numbersReconcile rule exists to prevent.
overviewReferenceRebuild.numbersStillReconcile: 4 = the Banners screen's own header count. 5 = the Approval Queue's five cards. 201 = the Dashboards screen. The queue section shows THREE of the five with a count badge and 'View all', which is the documented way to diverge: fewer rows plus a route, never a different set.
overviewReferenceRebuild.queuePreviewIsTheRealCard: The three preview cards are CLONES of the Approval Queue's own rows and resolve to mainComponent 1811:796 — the same card as My Requests. The reference's richer anatomy (severity badge + context chip + submitter) was NOT copied; our overline already carries #ref · type · requester. Reuse, not a lookalike.
overviewReferenceRebuild.activityFeedRestyled: Rows are now StatusDot + title + meta + relative time, right-aligned, and the status badge was dropped — the dot carries the semantic and the badge was saying the same thing twice. Dots are real StatusDot instances (online / neutral / away / busy), verified by reading each instance's variantProperties rather than judging colour from a screenshot. Rows were also REORDERED newest-first; the feed had #0421 (7:15 AM today) sitting below an entry from three days earlier.
overviewReferenceRebuild.gotchaResizeAfterFillResetsToFixed: The header's flexible spacer would not push 'View all' right. Cause: I set layoutSizingHorizontal='FILL' and THEN called resize(), which resets sizing to FIXED. Order is resize first, sizing second — the same rule already recorded for hug axes, in its other direction.
overviewReferenceRebuild.gotchaLintReadStaleWidthAndInventedAnOve: The lint reported 4 main-axis overflows on the activity rows (needs 856 in 832) and they were not real. A FILL child's .width property was stale by exactly one itemSpacing — computed before the third child was appended — while its absoluteBoundingBox was correct and the row summed to exactly 832. Nearly 'fixed' a defect that did not exist. Overflow must be measured from absoluteBoundingBox against the parent's content box, never from the width property of a FILL child. Eighth stale-sizing event in this file and the first where it produced a phantom FINDING rather than a phantom render.
overviewReferenceRebuild.verification: Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep: all zeros on both Admin Overview (2130:455) and Approval Queue (2122:3042). Every new itemSpacing bound to a real spacing/* token (12 bindings; three gaps of 3 snapped to spacing/0-5=2 rather than leaving an off-scale value). Donor holder frame removed.
overviewReferenceRebuild.openItems: Reference shows the submitter's ROLE ('Michael Ash, Managing Director'). Not added — it is a data field the system may not have, and inventing job titles for five mock users would have been fabricating a capability. Offer it if the directory exposes titles.
overviewReferenceRebuild.reviewActionAddedThenRemoved: ADDED then REMOVED the same day, owner's call. A per-card Review action (link Button in the meta column) was copied from the reference. It failed for a reason the reference could not show: OUR card already carries a status badge reading 'Needs review', so the right-hand column read 'Needs review / 09/02/2026 / Review' — the same word twice, 40px apart. The reference's badge said 'info', a severity, so 'Review' was the only verb on its card. Link style also gave it no affordance sitting under a date, and it broke parity with My Requests, where the whole card is the target and no row carries a button. The owner's question — 'what is the review in the lower right hand corner?' — was itself the finding. All 8 removed (5 queue, 3 overview preview); the card is the click target and the section's 'View all' carries the route to the queue. LESSON: before copying an affordance from a reference, check what the destination component already says in that slot — the reference's card and ours did not carry the same words.
overviewReferenceRebuild.gotchaMutateWhileIteratingAQuerySnapshot: Removing the buttons inside the same loop that iterated figma.currentPage.query('INSTANCE') threw 'The node with id ... does not exist' on a later .mainComponent read — the snapshot still held the button instances that had just been removed. Two-pass is the fix: materialise the target ids in a read-only pass, then mutate by id. Atomic execution meant nothing partial landed.

featuredIconConsistencySweep.trigger: Owner: 'in approval queue there is a general with the outline grey but the icon a warning color. I am finding some of those on the request flow as well.' Correct on both counts, and it was wider than the two spotted.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.canonicalMapping: The CHOOSER on Request Flow is the source of truth, because it is where the user learns the code: Dashboard = Color blue + Icon/layout-grid + glyph bound 59:70 · Banner/Notice = amber + Icon/bell + 59:62 · General Request = default(grey) + Icon/message-square + 35:65 · Feature Request = violet + Icon/flag + 59:72 · outcome success = 7:10.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.method: Measured every FeaturedIcon on BOTH pages and compared the nested glyph VECTOR's bound colour variable against the tile's own Color variant. Comparing bindings, not rendered pixels — the same reason a page-level probe gave a false all-fail earlier: variable modes cascade, but a binding id does not.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.found: 10 mismatches across 57 icons: 8 on Admin Flow, 2 on Request Flow. Worst cases were a General Request (grey tile) carrying the AMBER banner glyph on three separate screens, a Dashboard—Promote (blue tile) carrying the VIOLET feature glyph twice, and a Banner (amber tile) carrying the BLUE dashboard glyph twice.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.rootCause: The documented swapComponent binding bug, recurring. A card cloned from a donor of a different request type keeps the donor's glyph colour binding through the Color variant change — it is an inherited binding, not an override that a swap clears. Two of the ten were introduced by MY OWN clones earlier in this same session, which is the clearest evidence that cloning-then-recolouring is the mechanism.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.fix: Bound each offending glyph's stroke directly to the variable its tile colour implies, rather than rebuilding the icons. Verified: 17/17 on Admin Flow and 40/40 on Request Flow now agree.
featuredIconConsistencySweep.standingRule: After cloning any card that carries a FeaturedIcon, assert glyph-binding == tile-colour before calling the screen done. The eye catches roughly one in three of these — amber-on-grey is obvious, violet-on-blue is not.

activityBecameATable.trigger: Owner: 'I want the recent activity to be more like a table... this could get to be a lengthy list and might need a search. Imagine months worth of these requests.'
activityBecameATable.twoSurfacesNotOne: The overview keeps a five-row PREVIEW table with a View all route; the months-worth case got its own screen, 'Activity — all', cloned from the Dashboards screen so it inherits the search + filter bar and the 1008 table width. A landing page cannot host an unbounded log, and a log cannot live only as a preview.
activityBecameATable.builtFromTheTableComponents: Both tables are Table/HeaderCell + Table/Cell instances in the ui-table__header / ui-table__row idiom the Dashboards table established — not a second table shape. Cell Content variants carry the type: text, code (the #ref), badge (the event).
activityBecameATable.columnsDifferByWidthOnPurpose: Overview preview is five columns at 880 (When · Event · Reference · Request · Product). The full screen is six at 1008 and adds By. 'By' was DROPPED from the preview after measurement: at 880 six columns forced 'Priya Raman' and every date to wrap, and on the overview the actor is almost always 'You'. Column widths were settled by measuring rendered text height for wrap, not by eye — final state is zero wrapped cells on both.
activityBecameATable.referenceColumnNeeded128: At 104 and again at 120 the 'Reference' header wrapped, because a header cell carries a sort chevron plus gap that the label does not get to use. 'Inventory' needed 120 on the Dashboards table; 'Reference' needs 128. Budget the chevron when sizing any header.
activityBecameATable.filterIsByProductNotEvent: The ToggleGroup filters All / DART Central / Dartboards / Aiden. Product is the axis the admin's own permissions already follow, and a ToggleGroup instance has a fixed child count — four — which the four product scopes fit exactly and the six event types do not. Event stays a sortable column.
activityBecameATable.gotchaFontLoadIsPerFamilyNotPerScreen: First build threw 'Cannot write to node with unloaded font JetBrains Mono Regular'. Inter was loaded; the Code cell carrying the #ref is mono. Load every family the CELLS use, not the ones the page looks like it uses.
activityBecameATable.gotchaQuerySelectorCannotHoldASpace: node.query('TEXT[name=section heading]') silently matched nothing and returned null. Attribute values with spaces do not parse — use findOne with a predicate. Both failures were atomic, so nothing partial landed, which is the one mercy of use_figma erroring.
activityBecameATable.ownerEditedLive: Mid-build the owner rewrote the stat row directly in the file: four tiles rather than three, reordered with Pending approvals first, recoloured, captions changed to 'in Dart Central', and a new '12 Promoted Flags' — which restores the reference's promoted metric that I had substituted away. Left exactly as set. Worth noting the substitution was overridden: my reasoning was that the Dashboards table showed only one Promoted row, so the metric now wants a corroborating row on that table or it repeats the reconcile problem.
activityBecameATable.verification: Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep all zeros on Admin Overview (2130:455), Approval Queue (2122:3042) and Activity — all (2204:45476). Zero wrapped cells in both tables. No frame overlaps in the MANAGE section, which now holds Dashboards / Banners / Activity.

queueBecameAFlatTable.status: SHIPPED — 1008 queue and a full-column reference view, both lint-clean. Three follow-ups listed below.
queueBecameAFlatTable.trigger: Owner: admins do not need a per-product breakdown — 'requests are still handled as they come in'. Some admins hold one product, some hold all, but the work is a single stream. Wanted the queue to look like the Activity screen: one big table, product as a LABEL and a FILTER rather than a grouping, Jira-style, with row click to review and status changeable from the row.
queueBecameAFlatTable.shipped: Approval Queue (2122:3042) rebuilt: the three product GROUP frames are gone; content column widened 880 -> 1008; heading subtitle rewritten; filter bar cloned from the Activity screen (product ToggleGroup All / DART Central / Dartboards / Aiden, plus search); a 7-column table of 12 requests covering every status, not just pending.
queueBecameAFlatTable.columns: Ref (code) · Type · Request · Product · Submitted · Status (badge) · actions. Requester was DROPPED — it was not in the owner's list, eight columns do not fit at 1008 once each header carries a sort chevron, and the requester is still on the Activity table and the review screen.
queueBecameAFlatTable.scopeIsNowAFilterNotALayout: The permission story is unchanged — an admin still sees only the products they administer — but it is expressed by the product filter and the Product column rather than by grouping. This is the point of the owner's note: grouping implied you work product-by-product, and they do not.
queueBecameAFlatTable.statusVocabularyNowCoversTheWholeLifecyc: The table shows all requests, so the badges span Needs review (info-soft) · Waiting on requester (warning-soft) · Approved / Answered (success-soft) · Denied (error-soft) · Closed (soft). Closed is neutral, not red — a question that needed no answer is not a rejection, which is the rule already recorded for the Close action.
queueBecameAFlatTable.gotchaMaxWidthBeatsWidth: The content column would not go past 880 no matter how it was resized, because it carried an explicit maxWidth: 880 — the list content cap from when it held cards. A width is only a preferred width; the cap has to be NULLED. Exactly the trap CLAUDE.md records for .ui-command-dialog, in Figma rather than CSS. The Dashboards column had maxWidth null + FILL, which is what made the comparison decisive.
queueBecameAFlatTable.gotchaSizeColumnsFromMeasuredTextNotGues: Three rounds of nudging column widths by eye moved the wrap count around without fixing it. Reading each cell's NATURAL width (set textAutoResize WIDTH_AND_HEIGHT, measure, restore) gave the real numbers in one pass: Type 150, Request 251, Product 89, Submitted 80, plus a constant 32px cell padding. Those sum to 1015 against 1008 available, which is the actual finding — the layout is 7px over-subscribed and something has to give.
queueBecameAFlatTable.remainingDefects: RESOLVED — Submitted widened to 132; the waiting badge shortened to "Awaiting reply" so it stops spilling into the actions column.
notYetBuilt: The inline status-change affordance. Figma constraint found: a Table/Cell is an INSTANCE, so a chevron cannot be appended beside the badge — the status dropdown has to hang off the row's ⋯ actions button instead. A 'status menu open' frame was planned and not built; there is no DropdownMenu instance on the Admin Flow page to clone, so the donor must come from the Request Flow's scope-menu frame.
'Approval Queue — one product only' (2124:677) still shows the OLD grouped card layout and now contradicts the main screen.
'Approval Queue — nothing waiting' (2122:3220) empty-state copy still says nothing is waiting, which is wrong for a table that also lists decided requests.
Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep not re-run since the rebuild.
queueBecameAFlatTable.activeInactiveAxis: Owner asked for 'an active, inactive'. Implemented as the REQUEST LIFECYCLE, not the artifact's live state: Active = Needs review + Awaiting reply (still in the loop), Inactive = Approved / Denied / Answered / Closed (decided). Shipped as a SECOND ToggleGroup beside the product filter, same plain variant and therefore the same visual weight — the recorded trap is that a louder secondary axis out-ranks the scope. Also a State column in the wide view. FLAGGED TO OWNER: the other reading is the artifact — an approved banner that is currently displaying is 'active' until its end date passes, which is the vocabulary the Banners screen already uses. If that was the intent this axis means something different and needs redoing.
queueBecameAFlatTable.fullColumnSetView: New frame 'Approval Queue — full column set (no width limit)' (2218:1196), 2534 wide with a 2406 table — deliberately not a buildable screen but the column inventory at the width it actually needs, answering 'show everything you would add to this view'. 16 columns: Ref · State · Status · Type · Request · Product · Scope · Requester · Submitted · Updated · Assigned to · Starts · Ends · Inventory · Link · actions. Scope/Starts/Ends/Inventory/Link are pulled from the request-flow FORMS (banner scope and dates, promote window, dashboard inventory number and Tableau path), so most are legitimately EMPTY on a General Request — em-dashes are shown rather than blanks so the sparsity is visible, which is the argument for keeping them off the default view. An amber marker at table-x 1008 shows the 1440 cut-off: everything right of it scrolls. It lands mid-Scope, i.e. six and a half of sixteen columns fit unscrolled.
queueBecameAFlatTable.gotchaCannotRemoveAnInstanceChild: An empty Inventory cell could not be emptied by removing the nested Code instance — 'Removing this node is not allowed' for any child of an INSTANCE. The right move is the component's own axis: setProperties({Content:'text'}) switches the Table/Cell to its text variant, which then takes an em-dash. Fighting a component's structure usually means an axis exists that you have not used.
queueBecameAFlatTable.gotchaActionsColumnNeeds62: Both tables reported a real overflow: the actions cell at 60 has 32 padding, leaving 28 for a 30px icon button. The Dashboards table's 62 fits exactly. Copy the donor's width rather than rounding it down.
stillOpen: The row ⋯ menu has NO defined contents. It arrived with the cloned Dashboards actions cell. Because a Table/Cell is an INSTANCE, a chevron cannot be appended beside the status badge, so the inline status change has to live in this menu — it needs a 'status menu open' frame, with a DropdownMenu donor cloned from the Request Flow scope-menu (there is none on Admin Flow).
'Approval Queue — one product only' (2124:677) still shows the OLD grouped-card layout and now contradicts the flat table.
'Approval Queue — nothing waiting' (2122:3220) empty-state copy is wrong for a table that also lists decided requests.

flowClosure2026_09_02.what: Turned a set of admin screens into a flow. New: '② ADMIN — FLOW MAP', 'Request review — Banner', 'Approval Queue — status menu open', and two sidebar proofs. Repaired: the scoped-admin queue, the empty state, and the Dashboards status model.
flowClosure2026_09_02.navIsFlatAndTheREASONisPermissions: Owner: 'if I only give you access to Aiden but I have access to Aiden and Dartboards, I don't want the UI to look silly to you.' This is the governing rule, not a preference. A product-grouped nav CHANGES SHAPE with permissions — a single-product admin gets one lonely group and it reads as broken. A flat list does not: items you cannot use are hidden, the hierarchy never restructures. Product is a FILTER, never a level of nav. Proven by two frames, 'Admin sidebar — full access' (10 admin items) and '— Aiden only' (7): asserted programmatically that the Aiden list is an ORDERED SUBSET of the full one at the same flat depth, so only the count differs.
flowClosure2026_09_02.approveCreatesADraft: Owner decision. Approve creates the banner/dashboard as a DRAFT; the admin publishes separately. Matches the draft and scheduled states in the owner's own Banners design and keeps a human gate before anything goes platform-wide. Stated on the flow map: a request is WORK, the thing it produces is an ASSET; approving finishes the work and starts the asset without publishing it.

queueRefinements2026_09_03.answeredRetired: Owner: 'I don't think we need an answered status, what does that even mean, what is the actual status?' Correct. A question that was answered and one closed without an answer are both DONE, and the difference lives in the thread, not in a badge — a second terminal status only asked the admin to make a distinction the requester could not act on. Answered is gone; General requests end as Closed. The action bar changed with it: Answer became REPLY, because replying posts into the thread and does not end anything — Close is what ends it. Request statuses are now exactly five: Needs review · Awaiting reply · Approved · Denied · Closed, asserted by sweeping every Badge on the page.
queueRefinements2026_09_03.typesAreVerbFirst: 'Dashboard — Add' became 'Add Dashboard', likewise Promote and Remove. Verb-first scans faster in a table and it is also SHORTER — measured 132 against 150 — which paid for the wider Request # header. queueRefinements2026_09_03.refBecameRequestNumber: 'Ref' was terse to the point of being a puzzle. 'Request #' costs 20px (column 108 -> 128) and says what the column holds.
queueRefinements2026_09_03.sortIsNowExplicit: The queue was newest-first, which only LOOKED action-first because the pending items happened to be the newest. It is now genuinely sorted: Needs review, then Awaiting reply, then decided, newest within each group — and the subtitle says so. Same data, but the order is now a rule instead of a coincidence, which matters the first time an old request needs attention.
queueRefinements2026_09_03.overviewTableMatchesTheQueue: The overview's activity table now mirrors the queue's column rhythm — Request # leads, Event sits where Type does, When sits where Submitted does — and 'Reference' was renamed to match. The SORTS stay different on purpose: the queue is a work list ordered by what needs you, the activity table is a log ordered by what happened last. Two tables that look alike must earn the difference in wording, which is why the queue's subtitle states its order.
queueRefinements2026_09_03.docsFollowedTheChange: The READ FIRST panel still described a queue 'grouped by product', claimed only the request-review path was built, and said the queue 'shows only what is waiting' — three claims the rebuilt screens contradict. dataContract2026_09_03.what: New frame '③ DATA CONTRACT — request ↔ admin' (2260:2395, 1400 wide) in the documentation section. dataContract2026_09_03.theCoreIdea: One request has ONE canonical state; each side renders it with its own word. 'Needs YOUR review' and 'someone is reviewing it' are different sentences to different people, so the contract stores the canonical value and maps the label. Five states: in_review · awaiting_requester · approved · rejected · closed.
dataContract2026_09_03.assetStateIsASEPARATEAXIS: Section 4 exists because the two were being conflated. A REQUEST is work and ends in one of five states; a BANNER or DASHBOARD is an asset with its own lifecycle. Banner carries state (draft/scheduled/active/expired) AND a separate displaying boolean — the Switch — because an expired banner left switched on is still showing, which one combined status cannot express. Dashboard carries lifecycle AND health for the same reason: a published dashboard can be unreachable.
dataContract2026_09_03.auditingTheTwOFLOWSFOUNDREALDIVERGENCE: Reading the badges off both pages rather than trusting memory found four mismatches, and section 5 lists them with a decision for each. One was BROKEN: the Request Flow still showed 'Answered', which no admin action can produce since that status was retired. Fixed on both badges plus the behavior-spec prose. Two are cosmetic and mapped (Add Dashboard vs Dashboard — Add; Denied vs Rejected). One is DELIBERATE and marked keep (Needs review vs Pending review) — the audience difference is the point.
dataContract2026_09_03.gotchaRegexEditsOnProseNeedReadingBack: Replacing 'Answered' by regex produced 'Closed · Closed' in the requester behavior spec, because the separator was a middot my collapse pattern did not cover. Reading the paragraph back caught it; a second pass then left a trailing clause ('Closed is for one that needed no answer') that contradicted the sentence just inserted. A find-and-replace on PROSE has to be re-read as prose, not just re-scanned for the search term — the term being gone is not the same as the sentence being right.
dataContract2026_09_03.verification: Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep on the contract frame: all zeros. Zero occurrences of 'Answered' remain on either page. Request statuses across the Admin Flow sweep to exactly five.

sixStateModel2026_09_03.ownerModel: Owner traced the round trip and split the admin's first state in two: a request arrives NEW (nobody has read it) and returns as NEEDS REVIEW after the requester answers a question. Canonical states go from five to six: new · in_review · awaiting_requester · approved · rejected · closed.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.whyItIsWorthAState: New and Needs review are both the admin's turn, but they are different JOBS — cold triage versus re-reading a thread you already engaged with. Crucially the requester sees 'Pending review' for BOTH, because from their side nothing changed. That asymmetry is exactly what the canonical-value-plus-two-labels contract is for, and it is the cleanest justification for the split.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.storedNotDerived: Recommended and taken as a real stored state rather than deriving it (in_review AND no admin has posted yet). 'Show me everything untriaged' is a query you will want, and a derived state diverges the moment a second code path touches a request. new is reachable from exactly one place; in_review from two.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.sortInReviewAboveNew: Owner's call, and the arguable one. A returned request has already cost that person a round trip and is usually faster to finish because you know what you asked. The counter-argument — an SLA clock starting at submission makes untriaged the bigger risk — was put and not taken. The queue subtitle states the order so it is a rule rather than a coincidence of the data, which is the failure the previous sort had.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.badgeWeightCarriesTheDistinction: Needs review is info-SOFT (filled) and New is info-OUTLINE (bordered). Filled = act now, outline = queued and untouched. Same hue because both are your turn; different weight because one has already waited. Awaiting reply stays warning-soft — a different hue, because it is not your turn at all.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.propagation: Applied to the queue, the scoped-admin queue, the status-menu frame, the full-column-set reference, and the overview preview cards — whose order now mirrors the queue's top three. Docs updated: the contract's state and transition tables rebuilt around six states, the READ FIRST loop gained the New/Needs review hop with the reason for the sort, and the flow map's Active/Inactive paragraph rewritten. Asserted: all six labels present, and the only request-status badges anywhere on the page are those six.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.requesterSideUnchanged: No change was needed on the Request Flow: it shows 'Pending review' for both new and in_review already, which is what the model predicts. The only earlier fix there — retiring 'Answered' — is now marked RESOLVED in the divergences table.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.gotchaMyOwnCHECKLied: The flow-map edit reported as not applied because my verification regex, /Needs review, Awaiting reply\)/, matched inside the NEW string '(New, Needs review, Awaiting reply)'. The edit had worked. Third time this session a check of mine produced a false result — after the phantom overflow (stale width) and the phantom unreachable screen (exact-name match). A verification pattern needs to be able to FAIL on the new state, not merely match the old substring.
sixStateModel2026_09_03.verification: Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep: zero across all eight touched frames. Badge sweep returns exactly the six states and nothing else.

adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.editPatternIsADRAWER_establishedOnce: Owner chose a Drawer over the list. Built first, on Dashboards, deliberately — it applies to every page, so getting it right once pays four times. The list stays visible behind it, which is what keeps your place in a 201-row table. adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.accessControlWasReframedByTheOwner: Not 'who can view which dashboard'. Two things: who administers what (Lena administers Aiden alone — the exact case the flat-nav principle was built for), and LEVELED request access. Standard files General only; Contributor adds dashboard requests; Publisher adds Banner / Notice. The order is defensible rather than arbitrary: a banner displays to every user of a product, so the widest blast radius earns the highest bar. The request chooser reads this table, so a Standard user never SEES the Banner option rather than being refused after filling the form.
adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.promotionsNotFeatureFlags: Owner: 'these are one in the same' — a promotion is a browse-page highlight with a window, produced by an approved Promote request. So there is no Feature Flags page; the nav item wants renaming. A promotion is a WINDOW, not a switch: it ends on its date whether or not anyone remembers. adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.usageAnalyticsExposedACODEGAP: Built on Chart/Bar and Chart/Line, which exist in FIGMA ONLY — there is no src/components/Chart, the same position as Table. adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.customisableOverviewInThreeStates: Owner chose edit mode + widget picker. adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.gotchaComponentDefaultsRenderIfYouDoNotS: Input has NO Label text property — the label is a plain TEXT node inside the instance — so setProperties silently did nothing and every field rendered the master's demo label, 'Email address'. Input also has a Filled variant; without it, values render with placeholder styling. Second instance of this class today after the Switch's 'Enable two-factor auth'. adminSurfaceBuildOut2026_09_03.gotchaCodeChipsCannotWrapSoTheySetAFloor: The redirects table needed 1161 against 1008. twoEditPaths2026_09_03.ownerQuestion: 'A user submits a request to edit the dashboard with all the information inside the request — how can we link these so the admin doesn't have to put in all this information manually?' Plus: the admin also needs to edit without a request.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.theShapeIWasBuildingWasWrongForOnePath: The edit drawer alone treats every change as AUTHORING. When the change came from a request the admin's job is REVIEWING a proposal — a different task. So the Edit-request review screen is now a DIFF (field · current · proposed) rather than a flat field list, and approving carries the values forward. Retyping is not just tedious, it is how a proposal quietly becomes a different change.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.fromARequest: New 'Request review — Dashboard (edit)': three columns, changed rows in semibold foreground, unchanged rows reading 'no change' in muted. The action is 'Approve & apply'. It opens 'Dashboards — edit drawer (from request #0431)' already filled with the PROPOSED values, with 'was …' under each changed field so a bad proposal is still catchable at the last step. The admin may adjust before applying; if they do, the thread records that what shipped differs from what was asked.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.directly: The same drawer opened from the row, current values, no request behind it — and it SAYS so: 'Direct edit — no request. Recorded in Activity under your name.' plus a note that Activity is the only record. The path exists because a typo in a title should not need an approval round trip, but it has no requester, no thread and no approval, so it must not look identical to the request path.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.theRuleWorthKeeping: A request-driven edit is REVIEWED; a manual edit is AUTHORED. Same component, different job — different header, different provenance line, different verb (Apply & approve vs Save changes). If the two ever look the same, an admin cannot tell whether anyone asked for the change they are making.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.gotchaSettingFontNameDetachesTheTextStyl: Emphasising the changed values with node.fontName = Semi Bold produced three unstyled text nodes in the lint. A weight change has to come from a text STYLE (sm/leading-normal/Semibold), not a direct font assignment — otherwise the node silently leaves the type system while looking correct.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.verification: Eight-check lint + deep clip sweep: zero across the edit review, both drawers and the flow map. The flow map gained a 'TWO WAYS TO CHANGE SOMETHING' section stating both paths and why they must look different.
stillOpen: No 'what changed' entry is drawn in a dashboard's or banner's own Activity after either path — the record is asserted, not shown.
If the admin edits a proposal before submitting, the thread should show both what was asked and what shipped. Stated, not drawn.
A live-banner edit arguably deserves a stronger confirm than a plain Submit, since there is no draft state to fall back on. Raised, not decided.
Access Control, Promotions and Redirects still have no edit drawer at all.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.approveThenApply2026_09_03: Owner: 'you can't have approve on one and approve & apply on the other … approve as a step, then apply changes takes you to the dashboard page with the changes applied and then you hit submit.' Correct, and it exposed that I had broken a rule I had already written. APPROVE IS ONLY THE DECISION — it never changes anything a user can see — and whatever it produces always needs a second explicit step. That was already true for banners (approve -> draft -> publish); collapsing it into 'Approve & apply' for edits made the same button mean two different things depending on the screen, which quietly teaches that some approvals are safe to click and others ship immediately. Every review screen now carries the same verb.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.theUniformRule: Add Dashboard -> Approve -> DRAFT dashboard -> publish. Banner -> Approve -> DRAFT banner -> publish or schedule. Edit Dashboard -> Approve -> change STAGED -> 'Apply changes' opens the drawer prefilled -> Submit. Promote -> Approve -> SCHEDULED promotion -> starts on its date. General -> Reply, then Close -> produces nothing.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.approvedNotAppliedIsRealWork: The gap between the two steps is a state, so it is drawn: 'Request review — Dashboard (edit) · approved, not yet applied' carries a success-OUTLINE badge reading 'Approved · not applied' and a single forward action. Modelled as canonical approved plus an `applied` boolean rather than a seventh state — the same two-axis shape as the banner's state + displaying, and added to the contract's asset table. An approved edit nobody applied is outstanding work and must be visible as such.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.auditFoundRequesterAndDeveloperConflated: Sweeping names across the review screens found the Dashboard ones naming 'Jordan Mount' as the REQUESTER while the queue says Jordan Reyes — and Jordan Mount is the Developer name FIELD, a different person. Fixed on three frames (overline, thread, avatar initials) with the queue as the source of truth; the Add screen keeps Jordan Mount in the developer field, which was always correct. Found by auditing rather than by looking — the two names are equally plausible on screen.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.gotchaLoadEveryFontInTheSubtree: Writing a row into the contract's asset table failed on 'Cannot write to node with unloaded font JetBrains Mono Regular' — Inter was loaded, but the row's first cell is a code chip. Atomic, so nothing landed. Load every family the subtree uses, not the one you expect to write.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.bannerEditDiff2026_09_03: 'Request review — Banner (edit)' (2284:4615). Same three-column diff for the short fields — severity, scope, starts, ends — but the MESSAGE BODY does not go in a 300px column. Two paragraphs side by side in narrow columns is unreadable, and the message is the whole point of a banner, so it gets its own full-width stacked block: 'Currently displaying' in muted, 'Proposed' in semibold foreground, separated from the field rows by a hairline because it is a different kind of row. Short fields compare across; long text compares down.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.bannerEditsAreHigherStakesThanDashboardE: Stated on the screen rather than left to be discovered. A dashboard edit changes a library entry; a banner edit replaces what every user of that product is reading RIGHT NOW, with no draft in between — approve-then-draft cannot protect an already-live banner, because there is nowhere safe for the change to land. The demo also escalates Warning to Critical, which changes the banner's colour and moves it to the top of the stack, so the diff has to show severity as prominently as the text.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.bannerEditPathCompleted2026_09_03: 'Request review — Banner (edit) · approved, not yet applied' (2286:4692) and 'Banners — edit drawer (from request #0433)' (2287:4761). Both edit paths are now symmetric across the two types — review, approved-not-applied, prefilled drawer — asserted by name rather than assumed.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.theGapMEANSSOMETHINGDIFFERENTOnALiveBann: On a dashboard, 'Approved · not applied' is untidy. On a live banner it is the WRONG INFORMATION STAYING ON SCREEN: Dartboards users keep reading the two-hour wording at Warning severity while the approved Critical text sits unapplied. The copy says exactly that rather than reusing the dashboard's neutral wording, because this is the one place where the unapplied state is itself worth chasing. Same state, different urgency — and a shared component would have hidden that.
twoEditPaths2026_09_03.drawerNeededATextareaNotAnInput: The banner form is the first edit drawer with a long-text field, so the message uses Textarea (199:257) while everything else stays Input or NativeSelect. The 'was' hint under it is TRUNCATED with an ellipsis rather than repeating the full previous message — the review screen already showed the whole diff, and repeating it in the drawer would bury the field you are meant to be editing.

reorganisedByJourney2026_09_03.trigger: Owner: 'we have a lot of screens here … even I need help on the flow. How can we organize this to show a user flow from screen to screen?' Fair — 32 frames had accumulated in BUILD order, not in the order anyone walks them.
reorganisedByJourney2026_09_03.whatWasWrong: One frame (ADMIN — ACTION DIALOGS) was loose in no section at all. Section 3 held ten frames in one column with no logic, with two edit drawers stranded at the bottom away from the pages they belong to. Section 1 mixed the Overview with the queue and left its three customise states 5,700px below it. Section 2 mixed axes — types read left-to-right as parallel, edit variants read downward as a sequence, then the banner ones went rightward again.
reorganisedByJourney2026_09_03.sixStages: Sections are now the stages an admin moves through: 0 READ FIRST · 1 LAND · 2 TRIAGE · 3 DECIDE · 4 APPLY · 5 MANAGE · 6 CONFIGURE. Each stage is a vertical COLUMN and the stages run left to right, so scanning across the top shows the journey and scrolling down drills into one step. 200px between sections, which is the gap that stopped them overlapping last time.
reorganisedByJourney2026_09_03.everyFrameIsNumbered: N.M prefixes make the canvas self-indexing: 1.1 Admin Overview, 3.4 Request review — Dashboard (edit), 5.3 Promotions. The number is the link between the diagram and the canvas — no separate legend to keep in sync.
